what_failed: The first real guest Room Login (2026-08-26T10:23:03Z) verified correctly and was refused at the grant with package_not_offered_to_this_context. That reason was wrong in two ways: the failure was a PERMISSION error rather than an authorisation decision, and the offer lock it names was only the FIRST of five capabilities svc_scd does not hold. Driving the whole chain as the real service role against a production-like database found the rest.
capabilities_added: iam_v2.lock_auth_context_offer (0057) - the grant's offer row lock
iam_v2.lock_pms_interface_runtime (0058) - the grant-time linearization lock added by 0056
iam_v2.lock_stay and iam_v2.lock_origin_stay (0058) - the L1 Stay lock every auth path takes first

iam_v2.p3_feed_authorizes made SECURITY DEFINER (0058) - so the predicate reads pms_interface_runtime and stay_events as its owner instead of requiring scd to hold SELECT on the whole PMS event stream
EXECUTE on iam_v2.apply_entitlement_transition - the only writer of entitlement state
EXECUTE on iam_v2.authorize_entitlement_device and SELECT on iam_v2.entitlement_devices - the device binding, and the trigger that guards the session insert
privilege_model: No table UPDATE was granted. A row lock requires UPDATE in PostgreSQL, and each locked table is one scd must never write: auth_context_offers carries the fields the grant validates against, pms_interface_runtime is the feed health the authorisation is decided from, and stays is the stay engine's record of who is in the room. Each lock is therefore a scoped SECURITY DEFINER helper that takes it and returns nothing else. All six privileges live in the per-service Gate-P files, so a reconcile keeps them; scripts/gatep-grant-survives-reconcile.sh proves that across two consecutive reconciles.
